S3 Bucket Exposure Checker

Enter an S3 bucket name. This sends two plain, unsigned GET requests to the bucket's own REST endpoint — a ListBucket request and a GetBucketAcl request — and reports whether anonymous listing is enabled, and whether the ACL grants read or write access to AllUsers (anyone on the internet, no AWS account required) or AuthenticatedUsers (any AWS account holder anywhere — a commonly misunderstood setting). Object file contents are never fetched by this tool — only the key (file) names S3's own listing response already returns, and ACL grant metadata. See why S3 buckets end up publicly exposed for the common causes and the fix for each, or how this compares to checking by hand. Only run this against a bucket you own or are authorised to test.

Run the check

Enter a bucket name, then click Check.

Report

Prefer a CLI, or hit a CORS wall in the browser?

S3 buckets don't send permissive CORS headers by default, so a browser tab often cannot read a cross-origin response at all — you'll see a generic network error with no HTTP status. The CLI has no such restriction and is the one path guaranteed to complete: 

node check.mjs my-company-backups --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — exit code 1 if a finding is confirmed, so you can gate a deploy or a nightly audit on it.

Common questions

Does this tool show me the actual file contents in the bucket?

No, never. This tool only sends a ListBucket request (which returns object KEY NAMES, exactly the same names S3's own listing response includes) and a GetBucketAcl request (which returns grant metadata, never file content). It never fetches an object's bytes, and the report only ever displays key names and ACL grants -- never anything read from inside a file.

Why would a bucket end up publicly listable or writable in the first place?

Most commonly: a bucket created before S3's 2018 default-private ACL change and never revisited, a public-read ACL applied intentionally for static website hosting and left in place after the bucket started holding other data too, or S3 Block Public Access being disabled account-wide or bucket-wide for one legitimate reason and never re-enabled. AWS's own blog and IAM Access Analyzer exist specifically because this remains a common, ongoing misconfiguration.

How is this different from AWS's own tools (Trusted Advisor, IAM Access Analyzer)?

AWS's own tools check from the INSIDE -- they need you to be logged into the AWS account that owns the bucket. This tool checks from the OUTSIDE, the same unsigned, anonymous request any stranger on the internet can send with no AWS account or credentials at all -- useful for a quick self-check with no console access, or for a security researcher auditing a bucket they don't own an account for.

Is it safe to point this at a bucket name?

This tool sends only two ordinary, unsigned GET requests to the bucket name you give it -- the same requests any anonymous visitor, or curl, or the AWS CLI's --no-sign-request flag already makes. It never writes, uploads, or deletes anything, and it does not upload the bucket name or anything it finds to our servers when run in the browser. Still, only run this against a bucket you own or are authorised to test, the same caution you'd apply to any request tool aimed at someone else's infrastructure.

Does a clean report mean my bucket has no exposure at all?

It means the two requests this run made were both cleanly denied. It does not check bucket policies that grant access under conditions this tool's plain unsigned request would not trigger, does not check object-level ACLs on individual files, and only checks the one bucket name you give it. Treat a clean report as evidence about what this run actually found, not a full audit of the bucket or the account.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks two unsigned requests. It never writes, uploads, or deletes anything, never fetches an object's file content (only key names and ACL grant metadata), does not check bucket policies or object-level ACLs, and cannot see an exposure this run did not check for. A clean report describes what this run found, not a guarantee the bucket or account has no exposure.

You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for having authorisation to test any bucket you point it at. Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. Do not use it as a system of record.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every request goes straight from your browser to AWS — never through this site, and never logged or stored by us. The only thing stored is an anonymous local count of which features were used and the day — no bucket names, no findings, no account, no tracking cookies, no analytics vendor. Turn it off with the checkbox above.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

Also worth a pass on your stack: Supabase RLS checker and Firebase Rules checker cover the same "does this backend hand out data with no login" question for two other platforms, Dotenv Exposure checker and Git Exposure checker cover other static-file exposure classes, in the same "read what's actually there, name the exact evidence" shape as this tool. To check the bucket policy itself, paste it into the AWS IAM Policy Risk Check.

vs-checking-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to the S3 Bucket Exposure Checker

S3 Bucket Exposure Checker vs. checking by hand

Typing https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/ into a browser tab is a real, fast way to spot the single obvious case: a plainly readable ListBucketResult. It is also the method most developers already reach for first, and it genuinely works for that case.

CheckTyping the URL by handThis tool
Obvious public listingCatches itCatches it
ACL-based public read/write, with listing blockedNot checked -- a browser tab only sees the listing endpointA separate GetBucketAcl request checks read and write grants independently
Distinguishing AllUsers from AuthenticatedUsersEasy to read "AuthenticatedUsers" as "my own users"Named explicitly as "any AWS account holder", flagged as its own finding
A bucket outside us-east-1Can hit the wrong regional endpoint and see a confusing errorRetries once against the region S3 itself reports in the response header
Repeatable in a nightly audit or CIManual, point-in-timeCLI returns a real exit code

When to still just look

If you only need a one-off sanity check on a bucket name you already have open in a browser tab, looking is fine — it's free and you're already there, and it does catch the most common case (a plainly listable bucket). The gap this tool closes is coverage: the ACL check most people skip because it needs a second URL, the AuthenticatedUsers distinction most people don't know to look for, and an exit code a CI pipeline can act on.

Common questions

What does typing the bucket URL into a browser tab actually show you?

Typing https://bucket-name.s3.amazonaws.com/ into a browser tab is a fast, real check for the single obvious case: an AccessDenied XML error means listing is blocked, and a ListBucketResult means it is not. That's genuinely useful and free -- but it only checks listing, and only from whichever region endpoint your browser's DNS happens to resolve first.

Where does the by-hand check fall short?

Three ways this scripted check catches and a quick manual look easily misses: (1) It only checks listing, not the ACL -- a bucket can block anonymous listing while its ACL still grants AllUsers read or write access to individual objects by direct URL. (2) A grant to AuthenticatedUsers looks, at a glance, like it might mean 'my own team' -- this tool names it explicitly as 'any AWS account holder' so it is never mistaken for a scoped grant. (3) A bucket outside us-east-1 commonly needs a region-specific endpoint; a browser hitting the wrong one can get a confusing redirect or error that looks like 'blocked' when it isn't actually confirmed either way.

Why does this matter for a recurring audit, not just a one-time check?

A manual check is a point-in-time look at one bucket. A new bucket created from a script, a Block Public Access setting toggled off for a one-time migration and never reverted, or an ACL widened by a later object upload can reintroduce this exposure at any point. The CLI here returns a real exit code, so it can be wired into a nightly audit or a deploy pipeline, catching a regression the day it happens rather than the next time someone thinks to check by hand.

why-s3-buckets-end-up-public.html.text:
← Back to the S3 Bucket Exposure Checker

Why S3 buckets end up publicly exposed

A bucket only becomes a problem when it is listable, readable, or writable by someone with no relationship to your AWS account. There are a few common, independent ways that happens — fixing one does not fix the others.

1. Block Public Access is off, or was never turned on

S3's account-wide and bucket-level Block Public Access setting is the single strongest control: even if a bucket ACL or policy is later misconfigured to grant public access, Block Public Access overrides it and keeps the bucket private regardless. AWS has defaulted new buckets to Block Public Access ON since April 2023, but any bucket created before then, or any account where this was explicitly disabled for one legitimate reason and never re-enabled, can still be exposed. 

# Check the account-wide setting
aws s3control get-public-access-block --account-id YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID

# Check one bucket's own setting
aws s3api get-public-access-block --bucket my-bucket

# Turn it on for a bucket
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket my-bucket --public-access-block-configuration \
  BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true

2. A public-read grant left over from static website hosting

A bucket configured for public static website hosting needs a public-read grant — but that grant does not automatically scope itself to only the files meant to be public. If the same bucket later starts holding backups, exports, or logs alongside the website's assets, all of it inherits the same public-read grant. Move non-public data to a separate, private bucket rather than relying on object-level ACLs to carve out exceptions inside a public one.

3. A grant to the AuthenticatedUsers group

It is easy to read AuthenticatedUsers as "my own logged-in users" — it is not. It means any AWS account holder on the internet, with no relationship to your organisation at all. There is essentially no legitimate reason to grant this group anything; if a policy needs to scope access to your own team, use IAM roles or a bucket policy with a specific Principal, never this group.

4. Prefer bucket policies over ACLs entirely

AWS's current guidance recommends disabling ACLs altogether (S3 Object Ownership set to "Bucket owner enforced") and using IAM policies and bucket policies with explicit Principal elements instead — a policy is easier to audit than a set of per-object ACL grants, and it cannot be silently widened by a later object upload that specifies its own ACL. 

# Disable ACLs entirely (recommended for any bucket that does not need them)
aws s3api put-bucket-ownership-controls --bucket my-bucket \
  --ownership-controls Rules=[{ObjectOwnership=BucketOwnerEnforced}]

If this checker already found an exposure

Turn on Block Public Access first (step 1) — it is the fastest, broadest fix and overrides any ACL or policy underneath it. Then remove the specific ACL grant or bucket policy statement this checker named. If the bucket was listable, treat every object it held as potentially already accessed: check CloudTrail data events (if enabled) for anonymous GetObject calls, and rotate any credential or secret that may have been stored as an object in that bucket.

Run the S3 Bucket Exposure Checker against your bucket name to see which of these, if any, apply right now. Only run it against a bucket you own or are authorised to test.
